subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Anand, put the calculator down. I'm Tarun, and I want to tell you what my father's land meant to me.

He sold two acres so I could study engineering. I loved him for it, and it sat on my chest like a stone. When I began to want teaching instead, I heard "you owe this" in my head every night. For a year I obeyed and sulked.

Then I sat beside him on the charpai and said, "Baba, I'll always be grateful, and I'll look after you and Amma. But my gratitude isn't a bill you collect by choosing my job."

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I never thought of it like that. I only wanted you to have choices."

I became a teacher. He came to my first Annual Day, in his good shirt, and sat in the front row.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about Baba's sacrifice?
qa.a: Deeply loving and grateful, but also weighed down. It sat on Tarun's chest like a stone and Tarun heard "you owe this" every night.

qa.q: What did Tarun do to honour that gratitude without giving up the choice?
qa.a: Tarun thanked Baba openly and promised to look after both parents, but said plainly that gratitude is not a bill that decides Tarun's job.

qa.q: How did Tarun's father see the sacrifice?
qa.a: He had only wanted Tarun to have choices, and had never thought of it as a debt.

grounding: Tarun loves his parents and feels the weight of the father's sacrifice, and honours it without letting it become a debt that erases Tarun's choice.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Every Saturday Sofia folded sheets at her parents' laundry in Madrid, the laundry they had run for twenty years since arriving from Quito. Her mother's hands were cracked from hot water; her father still worked Sundays.
"They did all this so you could be a pharmacist," her cousin Dalia said, handing her a pile of towels. "You can't just switch to teaching."
Sofia pressed a crease flat. "I know what they gave up. I think about it every time I see Mamá's hands." She paused. "But if I choose pharmacy only to pay them back, I'll hate it, and they'll feel it."
"So you'll rebel?"
"No. I'll tell them the truth. That I'm grateful, and that teaching is what I'm good at."
That night she sat at the kitchen table with both parents and said exactly that. Her father was silent a long time. Her mother cried a little. Then her father asked, "Will you be happy?"
"Yes."
"Then show us the plan."

qa.q: How long had Sofia's parents run the laundry?
qa.a: Twenty years, since arriving from Quito.

qa.q: What did Sofia feel when she looked at her mother's hands?
qa.a: Deep gratitude and love, mixed with the weight of everything her parents gave up.

qa.q: How did Sofia honour her parents without treating it as a debt?
qa.a: She told them honestly that she was grateful and that teaching suits her, instead of obeying with resentment or rebelling.
Her father is silent a long time and her mother cries a little; then her father asks if she will be happy and wants to see the plan.

grounding: Shows love and gratitude for parents' sacrifice without treating it as a debt that erases one's own choice.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
In the common room of the nursing college hostel in Gangtok, Pema stared at the form for the overseas job fair. Her parents had sold half their cardamom field to pay her fees. On every call, Ama said, "Once you're working in Dubai, all our troubles will end."
"You've written your name four times and crossed it out four times," Gargi said.
"Because I want to work in the hill clinics here. And every time I think it, I feel like a thief."
"A thief of what?"
"Of their field."
Gargi put down her tea. "You can be grateful without living their plan. And you can't go to Dubai and resent them quietly for ten years."
Pema laughed shakily. "I'd be terrible at resenting quietly."
She didn't fill in the form. That evening she called home and told Ama and Apa what she wanted, and why, and that she would help the family in her own way. Ama said, "We'll talk more on Sunday." Pema took that as a start.

qa.q: What had Pema's parents sold to pay the fees?
Why did Pema say she felt "like a thief"?
qa.a: She felt guilty, as if choosing the hill clinics would waste the field her parents sold for her.

qa.q: What did Pema choose instead of obeying or rebelling?
qa.a: She left the form blank and called home to explain what she wanted and why, promising to help the family in her own way.

qa.q: How might Ama see Pema's call?
qa.a: Worried and unsettled, since she hoped Dubai would end their troubles, but open enough to talk more on Sunday.

grounding: Illustrates feeling the weight of parents' sacrifice and honouring gratitude without letting it erase one's own choice.
